overview.title: From Keras on Theano to TensorFlow, PyTorch and JAX, and three certainties about the future
overview.chapter: 3 Introduction to TensorFlow, PyTorch, JAX, and Keras
overview.section: 3.1 A brief history of deep learning frameworks
overview.main_topic: The history of deep learning frameworks from 2015 onward and the authors' predictions: Python has won, the world is multiframework (which favors Keras), and new hardware will have to fit existing frameworks
overview.central_idea: Keras launched in early 2015 on Theano; TensorFlow (late 2015) added large-scale distribution and brought deep learning to the mainstream, with Keras supporting it immediately; PyTorch (about a year later) drew on Chainer and NumPy-Autograd; Google's TPUs and the XLA compiler led to JAX. Today the four frameworks coexist, and the authors argue that Python is here to stay, that Keras's backend-agnostic design protects you in a multiframework world, and that new chips will adapt to existing frameworks.
overview.importance: This history explains the book's multiframework approach and its case for Keras as a stable layer above changing backends.
learning_objectives: Order the launches of Keras, TensorFlow, PyTorch and JAX and name what each drew on.
Explain the roles of TPUs and XLA in the story and how JAX relates to them.
State the authors' three 'certainties' and their argument for using Keras.
Distinguish the historical facts on the page from the authors' predictions.
prerequisites: The three key framework features and the early history up to Theano (p.85)

summary:
The page continues the history from p.85.

- Around 2013-2014, other GPU-enabled libraries were gaining popularity in computer vision: **Torch 7** (Lua-based) and **Caffe** (C++-based).
- **Keras** launched in **early 2015** as a higher-level, easier-to-use library **powered by Theano**, and quickly gained traction among the few thousand people doing deep learning then.
- In **late 2015** Google launched **TensorFlow**, which took many key ideas from Theano and added **large-scale distributed computation**. Its release was a "watershed moment" that brought deep learning into the mainstream developer zeitgeist. Keras added TensorFlow support immediately; by **mid-2016, over half of TensorFlow users** used it through Keras.
- About a year later, **Meta** (then Facebook) launched **PyTorch** in response, borrowing from **Chainer** (a niche, innovative framework from mid-2015, now dead) and **NumPy-Autograd** (a CPU-only autodiff library for NumPy, Maclaurin et al., 2014).
- Google released **TPUs** as an alternative to GPUs, with **XLA**, a high-performance compiler that lets TensorFlow run on TPUs. A few years later **Matthew Johnson**, one of the NumPy-Autograd developers, released **JAX** at Google as another way to use autodiff with XLA. It gained traction with researchers thanks to its minimalistic API and high scalability.
- Today Keras, TensorFlow, PyTorch and JAX are the top frameworks.

Asking what comes next (a new framework, language or hardware?), the authors give **three things they consider certain**:

1. **Python has won.** Its ML and data-science ecosystem has too much momentum; no new language will replace it, at least in the next 15 years.
2. **We're in a multiframework world.** All four frameworks are well established, and learning a bit of each is worthwhile, but new ones may still become popular (Apple's **MLX** is one possibility). Keras is an advantage here: existing Keras models should run on a new framework via a new Keras **backend**, providing future-proof stability as it has since 2015.
3. **New chips may arise** (AMD's GPU line likely has bright days ahead), but they will have to work with existing frameworks to gain traction, so new hardware is unlikely to disrupt your workflows.

paragraphs.what_it_says: About a year after TensorFlow, Meta (then Facebook) launched PyTorch, taking ideas from Chainer (mid-2015, niche, now dead) and NumPy-Autograd (CPU-only autodiff for NumPy, Maclaurin et al., 2014). Meanwhile Google released TPUs as an alternative to GPUs, with the XLA compiler enabling TensorFlow to run on them.
paragraphs.what_it_means: PyTorch inherited a define-by-run (eager) style from Chainer and a NumPy-like interface plus autodiff from NumPy-Autograd. In parallel, Google pursued specialized hardware (feature 2 of p.85) and a compiler to target it.

paragraphs.technical_idea: Beyond the book: XLA (Accelerated Linear Algebra) compiles graphs of tensor operations into fused, optimized kernels for CPUs, GPUs and TPUs.

paragraphs.what_it_says: Python has won: its ML and data-science ecosystem has too much momentum, and no new language will replace it, at least not in the next 15 years.

paragraphs.what_it_says: All four frameworks are well established and unlikely to disappear soon, so learning a bit of each is a good idea. New frameworks may still gain popularity, Apple's recently released MLX being one possible example. Keras is a considerable advantage in this context, since existing Keras models should run on a new framework via a new Keras backend; Keras will keep providing the future-proof stability it has offered since 2015.
paragraphs.what_it_means: Because Keras separates the model description from the engine executing it, a model written once can move between TensorFlow, PyTorch, JAX and potentially future backends. This decouples your code's lifetime from any single framework's popularity.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: This is the authors' core argument for the book's Keras-first approach while still teaching the backends.
paragraphs.technical_idea: Beyond the book: in Keras 3, the backend is selected with the KERAS_BACKEND environment variable (or the keras.json config file), and code written with keras.ops runs on any of them.

paragraphs.what_it_says: New chips may arise alongside NVIDIA GPUs and Google TPUs (AMD's GPUs likely have a bright future), but any new chip must work with existing frameworks to gain traction, so new hardware is unlikely to disrupt your workflows.

concepts.name: Keras backend
concepts.definition: The lower-level framework on which Keras runs; historically Theano, today TensorFlow, PyTorch or JAX, and potentially future frameworks.
concepts.intuition: Keras is the steering wheel; the backend is the engine, and engines can be swapped.
concepts.technical: Keras launched in 2015 powered by Theano, added TensorFlow support immediately, and is designed so a new backend can run existing Keras models.
concepts.significance: It is the authors' main reason why Keras offers future-proof stability in a multiframework world.
concepts.example: A model built with keras.layers and keras.ops can be trained with the JAX backend and later run with the PyTorch backend.
concepts.misconception: Keras is not tied to TensorFlow; that was one period of its history.

concepts.name: XLA
concepts.definition: A high-performance compiler developed to let TensorFlow run on TPUs, later used by JAX.
concepts.intuition: A translator that turns a sequence of tensor operations into fast, hardware-specific code.
concepts.technical: JAX was released 'as an alternative way to use autodifferentiation with XLA'.
concepts.significance: It links Google's specialized hardware to its frameworks and underpins JAX's scalability.
concepts.example: Fusing a matmul, a bias add and a relu into one kernel (an illustration, not from the book).
concepts.misconception: XLA is not a framework by itself; it is the compiler frameworks target.

concepts.name: Deep learning framework
concepts.definition: Software combining autodiff, accelerated tensor computation and distribution (p.85); today chiefly Keras, TensorFlow, PyTorch and JAX.
concepts.technical: Lineage on this page: Theano to Keras and TensorFlow; Chainer and NumPy-Autograd to PyTorch; NumPy-Autograd and XLA to JAX.
concepts.significance: The authors expect a lasting multiframework world.
concepts.example: Apple's MLX as a possible newcomer.
concepts.misconception: That one framework will eventually win; the authors expect several to coexist.

deeper.title: Lineage of ideas
deeper.body:
From the page:

- **Theano** (circa 2009) -> powered the first **Keras** (early 2015) and supplied many key ideas to **TensorFlow** (late 2015), which added large-scale distribution.
- **Chainer** (mid-2015) + **NumPy-Autograd** (2014) -> **PyTorch** (about a year after TensorFlow).
- **TPUs** + **XLA** (to run TensorFlow on TPUs) + a **NumPy-Autograd** developer (Matthew Johnson) -> **JAX**.
- **Keras** sits on top: Theano, then TensorFlow, today TensorFlow, PyTorch or JAX as backends.

deeper.title: Why abstraction layers protect you
deeper.body: Writing models in Keras is like writing documents in a standard file format rather than a single word processor's private one: when a better editor comes along, it learns to open the standard format, and your documents keep working. The authors' bet is that Keras plays that role for models, and frameworks play it for hardware.

misconceptions.claim: Keras was created as part of TensorFlow.
misconceptions.correction: Keras launched in early 2015 powered by Theano, before TensorFlow existed; it added TensorFlow support after TensorFlow's late-2015 release.

misconceptions.claim: JAX is unrelated to TensorFlow's ecosystem.
misconceptions.correction: JAX uses XLA, the compiler Google built to run TensorFlow on TPUs, and was released at Google.
They are the authors' predictions ('If you ask me'), argued from the history.

misconceptions.claim: New hardware will force you to rewrite your models.
misconceptions.correction: The authors argue new chips must work with existing frameworks to gain traction, so workflows are unlikely to be disrupted.

earlier.note: Three key features of frameworks; history up to Theano and ImageNet 2012.

later.note: 3.2: how the frameworks relate, Keras backends, and TensorFlow's release dates.

takeaways: Keras (early 2015) started on Theano; TensorFlow (late 2015) added large-scale distribution and went mainstream, and Keras supported it at once.
PyTorch (Meta, about a year later) drew on Chainer and NumPy-Autograd; JAX (Google) combined autodiff with the XLA compiler built for TPUs.
Today's top four: Keras, TensorFlow, PyTorch, JAX.
Authors' predictions: Python has won; the world is multiframework, which makes backend-agnostic Keras valuable; new chips will adapt to existing frameworks.

questions.question: Which library powered Keras when it launched in early 2015?
questions.explanation: Keras launched as a higher-level library powered by Theano. TensorFlow came in late 2015, PyTorch about a year after that, and JAX a few years later.

questions.question: Which two earlier projects did PyTorch take ideas from?
questions.explanation: Chainer was a niche but innovative framework from mid-2015; NumPy-Autograd was a 2014 CPU-only autodiff library for NumPy by Maclaurin et al.

questions.question: What was XLA originally developed for, according to the page?
options: To enable TensorFlow to run on TPUs
To run Lua code on GPUs
questions.answer: To enable TensorFlow to run on TPUs
questions.explanation: XLA is described as a high-performance compiler developed to enable TensorFlow to run on TPUs; JAX later used it. Autodiff for NumPy was NumPy-Autograd; Lua was Torch 7; nothing on the page ties XLA to PyTorch.

questions.question: Why do the authors consider using Keras a considerable advantage in a multiframework world?
questions.answer: Because Keras models can run on any backend, including future frameworks via a new Keras backend, so your models are not locked into one framework's fate; Keras has provided this stability since 2015.
questions.explanation: This is the argument of the second 'certainty' bullet, supported by the history of Keras moving from Theano to TensorFlow and beyond.

questions.question: What fact does the page give about Keras usage among TensorFlow users by mid-2016?
questions.answer: Over half of all TensorFlow users were using it through Keras.

questions.question: Why do the authors think new hardware is unlikely to disrupt your workflows?
questions.answer: Any new chip will have to work with the existing frameworks to gain traction, so code written against those frameworks keeps working.
questions.explanation: Frameworks act as the abstraction layer between models and hardware; the third bullet argues hardware adapts to them.

questions.question: Can you separate the page's historical claims from its predictions? List two of each.
questions.answer: Historical: TensorFlow launched in late 2015 with distributed computation; JAX was released by Matthew Johnson at Google. Predictions: Python will not be replaced in the next 15 years; new chips will have to work with existing frameworks.
questions.explanation: The shift is signalled by 'If you ask me, three things today are certain'.
